To convert to an IPL or CPL, the educator must meet the IPL or CPL requirements (including licensure exams) and have an EPP recommendation by June 30 of the third year; if not, the residency license expires. Because this educator has never taken the content test, the exam outcome must be confirmed for their license area before the June 30 deadline.

claims.text: A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets LICN-019 qualifications, so it can run for up to three years.

To convert a residency license to an IPL or CPL, the applicant must meet the IPL requirements in LICN-020 or the CPL requirements in LICN-024, and must be recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee.

If the applicant satisfies the conversion requirements by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If not, the residency license expires, and the IPL or CPL is effective on the date the applicant later satisfies the requirements.

For a teacher CPL, the applicant must satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, and must attempt the examinations at least once during the first year of licensure if the applicant did not satisfy them before receiving an IPL. A teacher CPL also requires at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and completion of a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies. The policies do not say whether residency license time counts as licensed teaching experience, so that needs confirmation.

The policies provide no extension or grace period beyond the June 30 deadline in LICN-019 §3(b). If the requirements are not met by then, the residency license expires, and the educator can convert later once the requirements are satisfied.

Years of experience decide the route. An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an initial professional license (IPL). An out-of-state applicant with more than three years may qualify for a continuing professional license (CPL). The applicant's stated 3 years is exactly three, which the policies do not place under either rule, so the route is not determined by the passages.

Under LICN-025 §1(a), to qualify for an IPL the applicant must either hold a license in the corresponding license areas in another jurisdiction, or have completed an EPP recognized by the jurisdiction where that EPP has its principal place of business. The policies do not define 'corresponding license areas', so whether the applicant's other-state EC license matches an NC EC area needs confirmation.

LICN-020 §1(b) separately allows an applicant who completed an EPP based outside North Carolina to qualify for an initial professional license, and LICN-020 §1(c) allows an applicant who holds a clear out-of-state license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction. Whether the EPP is recognized is a question for the analyst: LICN-001 §3(d) requires an EPP to be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority where it is based.

For any other EC area, the applicant must either achieve a passing score on an out-of-state exam for that area in the examining jurisdiction, or satisfy the NC exam requirements before or during the third year, provided they attempted the exams at least once during the first year.

NC test codes, as listed for the EC areas: Special Education: General Curriculum (code 88091) requires Foundational Knowledge Test 5355 with a score of 145, Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading with a score of 233, and Pearson Test 203 Mathematics Subtest (score 227) or 7813 CKT Math Subtest (score 150). Cross Categorical (code 88001) requires 5355 (score 145) and 5511 (score 148). The table lists the General Curriculum math row twice, so the analyst should confirm the requirement.

Out-of-state exam scores must be presented at the time of initial NC licensure to meet the IPL or CPL exam-based criteria, and an out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.

CPL route (more than three years of experience): the applicant must hold a clear license from another jurisdiction, meaning it is in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, not revoked or disciplined, has no pending unprofessional-conduct investigation, and was not surrendered under investigation. The applicant must also hold NBPTS certification, or the other jurisdiction's requirements must be substantially similar to NC's, including completion of a recognized EPP and a passing score on an out-of-state exam for each license area sought.

Fee: an out-of-state initial professional license application carries a fee of $100 under the fee schedule. The schedule's effective date is 2018-04-05, and it lists fees for applications opened effective January 1, 2017.

Application components include full legal name, SSN, date of birth, contact information, official transcripts for degrees, EPP completion documentation, a disclosure statement covering prior suspensions or revocations and criminal history, proof of any current valid out-of-state educator license, NBPTS certification proof if applicable, and documentation of licensure exam performance.

An IPL entitles the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina. The policies do not state a deadline for the applicant to obtain the license beyond the exam timing rules above.

If the applicant completed an EPP but has not satisfied the exam requirements, the policies define a limited license as a three-year renewable license for that situation, governed by LICN-023, which is not included in the provided passages beyond this definition.
